topic.name: Sums of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

question.text: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=x^2$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2, 4),$ then $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y=$
question.explanation:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y = x^2.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in[0, 2] \end{align}

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\,\mathbf j = \mathbf{i} + 2t\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

We can now evaluate the line integral: \begin{align*} \int\limits_C x\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y & = \int_0^2 x\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t + y\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] & = \int_0^2 \left(x\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + y\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] & = \int_0^2 t \cdot 1 + t^2 \cdot 2t\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = \int_0^2 t + 2t^3\,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \left[\frac{t^2}{2} + \frac{t^4}{2} \right]_0^2\\[5pt] & = \left[\dfrac{2^2}{2} + \dfrac{2^4}{2}\right] - [0]\\[5pt] & = 2 + 8\\[5pt] & = 10 \end{align*}

question.text: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overline{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(1,2)$ to the point $B(3, 4),$ then $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y=$
question.explanation:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = 3\,\mathbf{i} + 4\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) & = \mathbf{a} + t \, (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) \\[5pt] & = \mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j} + t(3\,\mathbf{i} + 4\,\mathbf{j} - (\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}))\\[5pt] & = \mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j} + t(2\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j})\\[5pt] & = (1+2t)\,\mathbf{i} + (2+2t)\,\mathbf{j}, \end{align} where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t) = 1+2t$ and $y(t) = 2 + 2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} \,\mathbf j = 2\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

We can now evaluate the line integral: \begin{align*} \int\limits_C x\,\mathrm{d}x + y\,\mathrm{d}y & = \int_0^1 x \, \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t + y \, \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 \left( x \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + y \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} \right) \mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] %& = \int_0^1 (x(t) \cdot x'(t) + y(t) \cdot y'(t) )\,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 (1+2t) \cdot 2 + (2+2t) \cdot 2 \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] %& = \int_0^1 2 + 4t + 4 + 4t \, \mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 6 + 8t \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \left[ 6t + 4t^2 \right]_0^1\\[5pt] & = \left[6(1) + 4(1)^2\right] - [0]\\[5pt] &= 10 \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \dfrac{x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}x + \dfrac{y}{x}\,\mathrm{d}y ,$ where $C$ is part of the circle $x^2+y^2 = 1$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ to the point $B\left( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right).$
question.explanation:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $1$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) & = x(t)\, \mathbf i + y(t)\, \mathbf j = \cos(t)\,\mathbf{i} + \sin(t)\,\mathbf{j}, \quad t\in\left[ \frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]. \end{align}

So, along the curve we have that $x(t) = \cos{t}$ and $y(t) = \sin{t}.$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\,\mathbf j = -\sin(t)\mathbf{i} + \cos(t)\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows: \begin{align*} \int\limits_C \dfrac{x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}x + \dfrac{y}{x}\,\mathrm{d}y & = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} \left(\dfrac{x}{y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + \dfrac{y}{x} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} \right) \textrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} \left(\dfrac{\cos{t}}{\sin{t}} \cdot (-\sin{t}) + \dfrac{\sin{t}}{\cos{t}} \cdot (\cos{t}) \right) \textrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} (-\cos t + \sin t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[5pt] & = \Big[ -\sin t - \cos t\Big]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\\[5pt] & = \left[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right] - \left[-\frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]\\[5pt] & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{1}{2} - \sqrt{2}\\[5pt] & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3} - 2\sqrt{2}+1). \end{align*}

question.text: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overline{MN}$ traversed from the point $M(0,1)$ to the point $N(3, 3),$ then $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^2\,\mathrm{d}x - y\,\mathrm{d}y=$
question.explanation:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = 3\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) & = \mathbf{a} + t \, (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) \\[5pt] & = \mathbf{j} + t(3\,\mathbf{i} + 3\,\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{j})\\[5pt] & = \mathbf{j} + t(3\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j})\\[5pt] & = 3t\,\mathbf{i} + (1+2t)\,\mathbf{j}, \end{align} where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t) = 3t$ and $y(t) = 1 + 2t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} \,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} \,\mathbf j = 3\,\mathbf{i} + 2\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

We can now evaluate the line integral: \begin{align*} \int\limits_C x^2\,\mathrm{d}x - y\,\mathrm{d}y & = \int_0^1 x^2 \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t - y \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 \left(x^2 \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} - y \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right) \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 (3t)^2 \cdot 3 - (1+2t) \cdot 2 \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 27t^2 - 2 - 4t \,\mathrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = \left[ 9t^3 - 2t - 2t^2 \right]_0^1\\[5pt] & = \left[9(1)^3 - 2(1) - 2(1)^2\right] - [0]\\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x +x\,\mathrm{d}y ,$ where $C$ is part of the circle $x^2+y^2 = 4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A\left( -2, 0\right)$ to the point $B\left( 0, -2\right).$
question.explanation:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $2$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

\begin{align} \mathbf{r}(t) & = x(t)\, \mathbf i + y(t)\, \mathbf j = 2\cos(t)\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin(t)\,\mathbf{j}, \quad t\in\left[ \pi, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]. \end{align}

So, along the curve we have that $x(t) = 2\cos{t}$ and $y(t) = 2\sin{t}.$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by \begin{align} \mathbf{r}'(t) & = \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\,\mathbf i + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\,\mathbf j = -2\sin(t)\,\mathbf{i} + 2\cos(t)\,\mathbf{j}. \end{align}

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows: \begin{align*} \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x +x\,\mathrm{d}y &= \int_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} y\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t + x\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\textrm d t}\,\textrm d t \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} \left(y\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\textrm d t} + x\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\textrm d t}\right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} \left( 2\sin{t}\cdot (-2\sin{t}) +2\cos{t}\cdot 2\cos{t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} \left( -4\sin^2{t} +4\cos^2{t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=4 \int_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} \left( \cos^2{t} -\sin^2{t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 4\int_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} \cos(2t)\, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 2 \sin{2t}\Big|_{\pi}^{3\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= 2\left[ \sin(3\pi) - \sin(2\pi) \right] \\[5pt] &=2(0-0) \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}
